title: Mix of Leisure Activities in Midlife Can Lower Dementia Risk, Study Finds
excerpt: A Trinity College Dublin study of 700 middle-aged adults found that combining physical, social, and intellectual activities boosts brain health and can overpower even the strongest genetic risk for Alzheimer's.
body:
• A new study of 700 adults aged 40-59 found that engaging in stimulating activities in midlife significantly boosts cognition, even in people with genetic risk for Alzheimer's.
  • Variety is critical — a combination of physical, social, and intellectual activities proved most effective at strengthening brain health.
  • Activities like socializing, playing music, creating art, exercising, reading, and traveling showed the strongest protective effects.
  • Depression and traumatic brain injury were identified as the two most harmful risk factors for brain health in midlife.

Picking up a musical instrument, traveling abroad, or simply going out to dinner with friends — these everyday pleasures may be among the most powerful tools for protecting against Alzheimer's disease and dementia, according to a study published in April 2026 in the Journal of Alzheimer's & Dementia: Diagnosis, Assessment & Disease Monitoring.

Researchers at Trinity College Dublin analyzed data from 700 people between 40 and 59 years of age with good brain health across Ireland and the U.K. who are part of a decade-long study. A third of the participants carry genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease.

The results were striking: engaging in physically, socially, and intellectually stimulating activities in middle age boosted brain activity significantly — even in those with elevated genetic risk.

Variety Is Key to Brain Protection

"We were surprised to see that stimulating everyday activities significantly boost cognition in midlife, decades before age-related cognitive decline sets in," said senior researcher Lorina Naci, a professor of psychology at Trinity College Dublin.

"Crucially, we saw that bigger benefits came from a mix of different activities, rather than one single one. Our results suggest that variety is key and that a combination of physical, social and mental stimulation is most effective for boosting brain health."

— Lorina Naci, Professor of Psychology, Trinity College Dublin

The activities that showed protective effects included socializing with family or friends, practicing a musical instrument, creating art, exercising, reading, learning a second language, and traveling. The study found that stimulating activity could overpower even the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's in shaping brain health during midlife.

What Harms the Brain Most

The study also identified the two most harmful risk factors for brain health: symptoms of depression and traumatic brain injury. Other damaging factors included diabetes, high blood pressure, poor sleep, and hearing loss.

These findings build on a large body of existing research. A 2022 meta-analysis published in Neurology, led by Lin Lu of Peking University Sixth Hospital, reviewed 38 studies involving more than 2.1 million people worldwide. That analysis found cognitive activities such as reading, handicrafts, and playing games or musical instruments were associated with a 23% reduced risk of dementia. Physical activities like walking, dancing, and swimming showed a 17% reduction, while social activities were linked to a 7% decrease.

Implications for the Indian Diaspora

The findings carry particular relevance for South Asian communities, where dementia prevalence is rising alongside aging populations. Research has shown that South Asians may face elevated risk due to higher rates of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and hypertension — all conditions the Trinity College study identified as harmful to brain health.

The emphasis on social engagement, learning new languages, and staying physically active aligns with cultural practices common in many diaspora households, from community gatherings and language classes to walking groups and musical traditions.

What's Next

Naci described the results as empowering. "This reframes brain health as something people can shape through lifestyle choices, encouraging earlier and more sustained engagement in enjoyable activities," she said.

She added that governments serious about reducing the future burden of dementia should prioritize mid-life lifestyle interventions, including mental health support, cardiovascular risk management, brain injury prevention, and access to lifelong learning and community engagement programs.

The researchers will continue to follow the 700 participants over time to track how these risk factors evolve as participants age.
